topic-2-1-1.title: One bit string, different interpretations
topic-2-1-1.caption: An encoding supplies meaning. The bits alone do not tell a machine whether to treat \(01000001\) as a number or a character.

topic-2-1-2.title: AND as a complete input–output specification
topic-2-1-2.caption: The truth table lists four possible inputs. Only the input \(11\) produces one; a circuit must implement all four rows.

topic-2-1-3.title: OR written as a polynomial over bits
topic-2-1-3.caption: All additions are modulo two. The polynomial \(x+y+xy\) reproduces OR on Boolean inputs; its interpretation depends on this arithmetic.

topic-2-2-3.title: Three different inputs merge
topic-2-2-3.caption: The AND gate maps \(00\), \(01\), and \(10\) to the same output. Output zero cannot identify which of these inputs occurred.

topic-2-3-1.title: Resetting an unknown bit
topic-2-3-1.caption: Both possible logical inputs are reset to zero. For erasure of one equally likely bit in the standard isothermal setting, the minimum heat delivered to the environment is kBT ln 2.

topic-2-3-2.title: Logical and physical questions are separate
topic-2-3-2.caption: A reversible truth table settles whether the input is recoverable. It does not specify the energy dissipated by a particular physical device.

topic-2-3-3.title: Preserve the input; update the target
topic-2-3-3.caption: Configurations are written \(xt\), here with \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\). \(U_f\) flips the target exactly when \(f(x)=1\), and applying it twice returns every configuration.

topic-2-4-1.title: A controlled operation has two branches
topic-2-4-1.caption: CNOT keeps the control, the first bit, and flips the target when the control is \(1\): \(10\) and \(11\) exchange. Exactly one arrow enters each configuration, so the step can be undone.

topic-4-1-1.title: Ket notation and coordinates
topic-4-1-1.caption: The two coordinates are ordered by the selected basis. The coefficients belong to basis vectors, not to two simultaneous measurement outcomes.

topic-4-2-1.title: Normalization of a state vector
topic-4-2-1.caption: The vector \((3,4)^T\) has norm five. Dividing it by five gives a unit vector, whose squared coordinates sum to one.

topic-6-1-1.title: Local labels form joint basis labels
topic-6-1-1.caption: The joint basis has one label for every pair of local labels. This is the Cartesian arrangement of tensor-product basis vectors, not a mixture.

topic-6-1-2.title: A superposition can still factor
topic-6-1-2.caption: Both terms share the same second-qubit state. Factoring it out shows that this pure state is a product, despite having two nonzero amplitudes.

topic-6-1-3.title: Description size and measurement output
topic-6-1-3.caption: The number of basis coefficients doubles with each added qubit. One computational-basis measurement still returns only one n-bit label.

topic-6-2-2.title: The Bell coefficients cannot be a product
topic-6-2-2.caption: A product \((a\ket0+b\ket1)(c\ket0+d\ket1)\) would require \(ac\) and \(bd\) nonzero. Then all four factors are nonzero, contradicting \(ad=bc=0\).

topic-6-2-3.title: Sum joint probabilities to get a marginal
topic-6-2-3.caption: For the Bell state, the row sums give the first-qubit probabilities. Conditional on the first bit being zero, only the \(00\) entry remains possible.

topic-6-3-1.title: CNOT copies labels, not arbitrary states
topic-6-3-1.caption: With a blank target, CNOT carries the amplitude \(\alpha\) of \(00\) to \(00\) and the amplitude \(\beta\) of \(10\) to \(11\). The result \(\alpha\ket{00}+\beta\ket{11}\) is not two copies of \(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) unless \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) is zero.

topic-6-3-2.title: Cloning would have to preserve an impossible overlap
topic-6-3-2.caption: Let \(c=\braket\psi\phi\). A unitary cloning map would preserve input overlap \(c\), while two copies have overlap \(c^2\). The value \(1/\sqrt2\) cannot satisfy that requirement.

topic-6-3-3.title: Local statistics do not carry a distant outcome
topic-6-3-3.caption: For the Bell pair, either local computational-basis distribution is fair. Learning the remote outcome permits conditioning; without it, the local distribution remains unchanged.

topic-6-4-1.title: Teleportation consumes shared resources
topic-6-4-1.caption: Alice and Bob first share a Bell pair. Alice’s joint measurement and two-bit message allow Bob to select the correction; the shared pair is consumed in transferring the input state.

topic-6-4-3.title: A state is transferred, not a second copy retained
topic-6-4-3.caption: The two-bit message selects a correction using a previously shared Bell pair. It is not a classical list of the unknown amplitudes.

topic-7-1-1.title: Four truth tables, two classes
topic-7-1-1.caption: Deutsch’s task asks whether the two outputs agree. It does not require identifying which truth table in a class was supplied.

topic-7-1-2.title: One observed value leaves an ambiguity
topic-7-1-2.caption: If a classical query returns \(f(0)=0\), both a constant and a balanced truth table remain possible. A second value is needed for an exact classical answer.

topic-7-1-3.title: The target update is a permutation
topic-7-1-3.caption: Configurations are written \(xy\), here with \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\). Where \(f(x)=1\) the two target values exchange; elsewhere nothing moves. One arrow enters each configuration, so \(U_f\) is reversible even when \(f\) is not one-to-one.

topic-7-2-1.title: Apply the oracle term by term
topic-7-2-1.caption: With \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\), each amplitude follows its own arrow. The input superposition with a blank target becomes \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\): the target is now correlated with the input.

topic-7-2-2.title: A joint measurement returns one pair
topic-7-2-2.caption: For \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), a computational-basis measurement samples one of these four labels. It does not output the full list of amplitudes.

topic-7-2-3.title: Workspace can distinguish input branches
topic-7-2-3.caption: Different workspace records can prevent the desired input interference. The shared-workspace example factors; the branch-record example does not. The common normalization factor \(1/\sqrt2\) is omitted in the labels.

topic-7-3-1.title: The target eigenvalue supplies the sign
topic-7-3-1.caption: A bit flip moves each amplitude to the other configuration. For \(\ket-\) the result is \(-\ket-\): the target is unchanged apart from a sign, which the oracle can pass to the input.

topic-7-3-3.title: Compute, mark, then clear the record
topic-7-3-3.caption: For a basis input \(x\), compute \(f(x)\) into clean workspace, apply \(Z\) to that bit, and reverse the computation. The function-dependent sign remains while the workspace returns to zero.

topic-7-4-1.title: A sign pattern becomes a measured bit
topic-7-4-1.caption: The final \(H\) sends each signed amplitude along two arrows. At \(0\) the contributions add and at \(1\) they subtract, so equal signs give \(0\) with certainty and opposite signs give \(1\).

topic-7-4-3.title: Every stage contributes to correctness
topic-7-4-3.caption: The target \(\ket-\) lets the oracle encode a phase without keeping an input-dependent target record. The final \(H\) converts that phase into the answer.

topic-9-1-1.title: A predicate tests one candidate
topic-9-1-1.caption: In this four-item example only \(11\) is marked. Testing a supplied candidate is different from locating the successful one.

topic-9-1-2.title: Marking changes a sign, not a probability
topic-9-1-2.caption: The oracle keeps every configuration and multiplies the amplitude of the marked item \(11\) by \(-1\). Every immediate measurement probability stays \(1/4\), so another operation is needed to turn the sign into an advantage.

topic-9-2-1.title: Group coordinates into good and bad directions
topic-9-2-1.caption: For one marked item among four, \(\ket{G}=\ket{11}\) and \(\ket{B}=(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt3\). These orthogonal directions contain the initial state and the entire ideal search trajectory.

topic-9-2-2.title: Initial amplitude fixes the angle
topic-9-2-2.caption: With one marked item among four, \(\sin\theta=1/2\), so \(\theta=30^\circ\). The good amplitude is the vertical component; the success probability is its square.

topic-9-2-3.title: Two reflections advance the state
topic-9-2-3.caption: For \(\theta=30^\circ\), the initial state is at \(30^\circ\). The oracle reflects it to \(-30^\circ\) about the bad axis; reflection about the initial direction then sends it to \(90^\circ\). These are real coordinates in the good/bad plane.

topic-9-3-1.title: Success oscillates with iteration count
topic-9-3-1.caption: For \(N=4\) and \(M=1\), \(p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\pi/6)\). One iteration is ideal, but the next two return to probability \(1/4\). Stopping is part of the algorithm.

topic-9-3-3.title: Measure a candidate, then verify it
topic-9-3-3.caption: A failed verification rejects that candidate, not every possible candidate. With an unknown marked fraction, the schedule must choose how long to search before measuring again.

topic-9-4-1.title: Amplification uses the prepared success weight
topic-9-4-1.caption: A nonuniform preparation can still be resolved into normalized good and bad components. This example has \(p=1/4\), so its amplitudes are \(1/2\) and \(\sqrt3/2\) regardless of how many underlying labels contribute.

topic-9-4-3.title: Count the work inside each amplification round
topic-9-4-3.caption: For small \(p\), the improvement concerns repeated use of coherent preparation and the success test. Their implementation costs must be included.

topic-8-1-1.title: Time order and matrix order
topic-8-1-1.caption: The circuit applies \(H\) first and \(Z\) second, as the columns run from left to right. The combined operator is written \(ZH\): on a column vector the rightmost matrix acts first.

topic-8-1-2.title: Open a query box to count its gates
topic-8-1-2.caption: A query diagram counts uses of an oracle. Replacing each box by a circuit exposes the gate cost, plus any operations between calls.

topic-8-1-3.title: A measured bit selects a correction
topic-8-1-3.caption: Classical control uses a recorded outcome. It selects a branch after measurement rather than preserving a coherent superposition of both control alternatives.

topic-8-2-1.title: Gates act differently on different inputs
topic-8-2-1.caption: \(X\) exchanges basis labels; \(Z\) changes one sign; \(H\) changes basis. Their action on arbitrary superpositions follows by linearity.

topic-8-3-1.title: Local gates preserve a product form
topic-8-3-1.caption: Applying \(A\) to one qubit and \(B\) to the other gives \((A\ket\psi)\otimes(B\ket\phi)\). Starting with a product, local unitary gates alone cannot create entanglement.

topic-8-3-2.title: One route to universality
topic-8-3-2.caption: Arbitrary one-qubit unitaries together with CNOT suffice to construct arbitrary finite-register unitaries. A chosen finite gate alphabet instead generally requires approximation.

topic-8-3-3.title: Approximation includes a tolerance
topic-8-3-3.caption: The task is to find a finite circuit \(V\) close enough to a target \(U\). The tolerance controls acceptable error and affects the required circuit length.

topic-8-4-1.title: The same gate count can give different depths
topic-8-4-1.caption: Four independent gates on four wires can occupy one layer. Four dependent gates on one wire require four layers. Parallelism may use more workspace.
rows: One gate on each of four wires
Four gates in sequence on one wire

topic-8-4-2.title: Connectivity can require moving information
topic-8-4-2.caption: On a three-site line only neighboring sites interact directly. To act on logical qubits A and C, swap A next to C, apply the gate, and restore the placement if needed.
rows:
SWAP first pair
B — A — C

topic-8-4-3.title: A worst-case error budget
topic-8-4-3.caption: For ideal and implemented unitary gates with operator-norm error at most ε per gate, a telescoping bound gives total error at most mε. The bound is not a claim that all errors add with the same sign in a particular run.

topic-10-1-1.title: Input value is not input length
topic-10-1-1.caption: Binary encoding uses logarithmically many bits. A cost proportional to the integer’s value can therefore be exponential in the number of input bits.

topic-10-1-2.title: Asymptotic order and finite costs
topic-10-1-2.caption: The linear algorithm with a large constant eventually wins, but not for every input size. Big-O notation describes growth, not a complete timing prediction.

topic-10-1-3.title: Fewer queries can cost more gates
topic-10-1-3.caption: These totals count only the gates inside query calls. Preparation and other gates must still be added for a full comparison.

topic-10-2-1.title: An efficient reduction transfers a solver
topic-10-2-1.caption: If task \(A\) reduces efficiently to task \(B\), an efficient solver for \(B\) would yield one for \(A\). The arrow describes converting instances, not proving that such a solver exists.

topic-10-2-2.title: Bounded error is a per-input requirement
topic-10-2-2.caption: Both classes concern polynomial-time decision procedures with a bounded error on every allowed input. The computational model differs.

topic-10-2-3.title: Different tasks offer different structure
topic-10-2-3.caption: Factoring uses arithmetic structure; unstructured search assumes only oracle access to a predicate. A lower bound for the latter is not a lower bound for every structured problem.

topic-10-3-1.title: Two directions of a complexity argument
topic-10-3-1.caption: A construction proves that a task can be solved within a cost. A lower bound must cover every permitted algorithm in the stated model.

topic-10-3-2.title: Search upper and lower bounds meet
topic-10-3-2.caption: For one marked item and constant success in the unstructured quantum query model, Grover’s \(O(\sqrt N)\) upper bound and the \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\) lower bound give \(\Theta(\sqrt N)\) query complexity.

topic-10-3-3.title: Combine a model bound with a function bound
topic-10-3-3.caption: The query model limits acceptance degree to \(2T\). If approximating the requested function requires degree \(d\), then \(2T\ge d\). The approximate-degree theorem is a separate ingredient.

topic-10-4-1.title: Follow the costs around the algorithm
topic-10-4-1.caption: An advantage claim must include the access assumptions and success criterion. Expensive preparation or readout can dominate a reduction in oracle calls.

topic-10-4-2.title: Three different limitations
topic-10-4-2.caption: A faster implementation does not turn an undecidable task into a decidable one, nor make all amplitudes available from a single measurement.

topic-10-4-3.title: Algorithmic structure and physical reliability
topic-10-4-3.caption: Period finding concerns making structure observable; error correction concerns protecting a computation from faults. A useful large computation needs both suitable algorithms and sufficiently reliable operations.

appendix-a.title: A stack remembers the unmatched prefix
appendix-a.caption: Reading \(aabb\) pushes for each \(a\) and pops for each \(b\). The empty stack at the end certifies matching counts in this example; checking order is also required.

appendix-b.title: A derivation generates a string
appendix-b.caption: Apply \(S\to aSb\) twice, then \(S\to\) empty string. This demonstrates generation of \(aabb\); it does not yet give a procedure for rejecting arbitrary strings.

appendix-c.title: Use conjugation when normalizing
appendix-c.caption: For the complex vector \((3,4i)\), the squared norm is \(9+16=25\). Dividing by five gives a unit vector; the imaginary coordinate contributes positively to its norm.

appendix-d.title: Different ensembles can yield the same density matrix
appendix-d.caption: An equal mixture of \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) and an equal mixture of \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\) both yield \(I/2\). No measurement on the qubit alone identifies which ensemble was used.

appendix-e.title: Queries can increase polynomial degree
appendix-e.caption: Starting from amplitudes independent of hidden input bits, each Boolean query raises their degree by at most one. Squaring magnitudes gives the factor of two for acceptance probabilities.

topic-3-2-1.title: The product rule along one path
topic-3-2-1.caption: The weight of the path \(i\to j\to k\) is the product of its two transition weights.

topic-3-2-2.title: Sum the paths to a common endpoint
topic-3-2-2.caption: Each route passes through an intermediate configuration \(j\). Multiply along each route, then sum over all intermediate configurations; the dots stand for any additional routes.

topic-3-2-3.title: Update one component of the state
topic-3-2-3.caption: Each initial weight \(v_i\) contributes \(w(i\to j)v_i\) to the new weight at \(j\). The new state contains one such sum for every output configuration.

topic-3-3-1.title: Signs multiply along a path
topic-3-3-1.caption: Each row is a path through configurations \(i\), \(j\), and \(k\), with transition weights on the arrows. One negative arrow gives path weight \(-1/4\); two negative arrows give path weight \(+1/4\). The rows are separate examples.

topic-3-3-2.title: Cancellation at a common endpoint
topic-3-3-2.caption: Two paths to the same configuration \(k\) contribute \(ca\) and \(db\). With \(a=b=c=1/2\) and \(d=-1/2\), the contributions cancel although both paths are present.

topic-3-4-1.title: Magnitude and phase of an amplitude
topic-3-4-1.caption: The amplitude \(z=re^{i\phi}\) is a vector of length \(r\) at angle \(\phi\) in the complex plane. Its real and imaginary components are \(r\cos\phi\) and \(r\sin\phi\); its squared magnitude is \(r^2\).

topic-3-4-2.title: Relative phase changes how paths combine
topic-3-4-2.caption: Prepare equal-magnitude amplitudes with relative phase \(\phi\), then apply \(H\). Only the routes to final configuration zero are shown. The phase changes their sum, even though it leaves the initial probabilities unchanged.

topic-3-4-3.title: A record separates the final configurations
topic-3-4-3.caption: The second qubit records the intermediate value of the first. The two routes shown both give first-qubit outcome one, but end in different joint configurations, \(10\) and \(11\). Their amplitudes cannot cancel: add their squared magnitudes when ignoring the record. The routes to first-qubit outcome zero are omitted.

topic-4-2-2.title: Measurement and its conditional state
topic-4-2-2.caption: For \(\ket\psi=(\sqrt3/2)\ket0+(1/2)\ket1\), the first measurement gives the indicated probabilities. Each branch leaves a definite state, so an immediate repeat gives the same result.

notes.text: Arrow labels are probabilities; nodes are conditional states.

topic-3-1-1.title: A state of one bit
topic-3-1-1.caption: Each configuration carries a weight. The state is the pair of weights \(v_0\) and \(v_1\).

topic-3-1-3.title: RESET merges two configurations
topic-3-1-3.caption: RESET sends both configurations to \(0\). A run that reaches \(0\) does not record where it started, so RESET is deterministic but not reversible.
